Cold was the word of the day.  We caught a ride with Brad Sills up to the Callaghan Country Lodge.  The north facing slopes in the area looked thin, shady, and dreadfully cold, so we climbed up the north side of the valley for some sun.  Temperatures were warmer up high, but the ridge crests were really wind swept.  At the end of the day we skied back down to Callaghan Lake off the north side of the ridge, which was an excellent despite the low snowpack.

column2: Looking up at the start of Carumba Crags. There was a fixed line, but there was a core shot near the bottom and I couldn't see enough of the top of it to trust it, so I decided to just ignore it.
Does Sarah look just a bit scared?

About 45m up, standing on a mediocre angle, I could just barely touch this old crusty rap tat hanging off the chopped off remains of a bush. There was so much dirt over everything else I could use that I had no choice but to use it.

I got one of my own slings on the bush remains and was starting to feel a little better when it started making cracking sounds. At that point I got a fist in between the rock and the dirt with one hand, jammed the other into the dirt and tried to pull myself up.

All of a sudden, the muffled popping sound of tiny roots breaking put me into a state of terror. I yelled "[url=http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dgx1sSfriIA]oh fudge[/url]" loud enough for all of Squamish to hear.
I was caught momentarily on my last angle, but I had an enormous block of dirt clipped to my rope coming towards me.
I got smashed pretty well by the falling wall of dirt. As an added bonus, it pulled out my angle.
My rack hung up on this spindly little cedar, which also happened to be my last "placement" that I hadn't back-cleaned.
When the falling dirt block ran out of rope, it dislocated my shoulder, popped me out of my rack and somehow dislodged my rack from the cedar at the same time.
I was now headed down towards my steadily disintegrating dirt block head first.
I stuck into the dirt block like a lawn dart.
The rope was still under load, though, so it folded me over backwards.
I wasn't able to wrest my head from the mess--only after I was lowered a ways was I able to extract myself.
I was somewhat disheveled when I got to the ground, but was pretty stoked to be off the wall.
By the time I got to the ground, almost all of the dirt had fallen out of my attacker, leaving a huge ball of roots. It was still to heavy for me to lift it up like a prize bass, though.
Sarah shows off the pile of dirt I made. The pile is only a portion of what fell off the terrible block--many of the larger pieces landed a ways out.

We were waiting at the col when we had to turn around and help Nacho. His leg was hit by a rock (just over the size of a head. There aren't normally rock falls in this area so Nacho was quite unlucky.
We called the Gendarmerie de montange (search and rescue in Charmonix). The helicopter arrived in a few minutes and they told us we didn't even have to move to a flat spot. Someone was lowered out of the helicopter already equiped with crampons and Nacho and Loli were all taken up into the helicopter.

Tobias skiing down after summiting on day 3. In behind are the large seracs. These seracs also fell, caused an avalanche and killed a bunch of people. Most guides in Charmonix wont go up the normal route anymore to avoid being under the seracs for a long time.

Weather is getting bad and we are heading back over la Jonction glacier. Sorry for the bad photo, this is a bridge we had to walk over only one meter wide, maybe less, with large crevasses on each side.

Missed the last gondola down at 5:30 and stayed at the Refuge du Plan. Well worth it the hut gardien is the best host I have found at a hut and he cooks really well. Walked down from the hut the next day (~2.5 hrs to Charmonix)

column2: Kala Patthar is the best and closest viewpoint of Mount Everest that is achievable without having mountaineering skills. At a peak altitude of 5550m, the air is thin - 50% of what is at sea level. The slightest exertion going uphill will send your lungs gasping for air. We woke up early on a foggy Sunday, May 8 to ascend it. Our guide said it was about -10 to -15C. We were freezing. But alas, we fought on to be at one of the highest places on the planet... and to be next to Mount Everest.

By: Frederick Lin

On days when it is unsafe to climb to a new permanent altitude, we do acclimitization hikes to help the body adjust to decreasing levels of oxygen. These hikes are done when we hike higher for the day, but descend to sleep. Here, we are doing an acclimatization hike from Dingboche (4500m) to Chukhung (4700m) and back to Dingboche.  In Nepal trekking to Everest Base Camp.

By: Frederick Lin

Tengobche Monastery (3867m), also known as Dawa Choling Gompa, is located in the village of Tengboche. It is the largest gompa in the Khumbu valley. It is also a very difficult hike from Namche (3440m) for trekkers that are in the process of acclimatizing, with most of the elevation gain occuring in the last stretch.

We had the opportunity to sit in on one of two daily prayers performed at the monestary. Many people ask for prayers, including members of expedition teams on their way up to summit Everest.

We found this neat little talus cave near the base of one of our climbs at Skaha Bluffs on Easter day. We hit a stroke of luck and rappelled in at just the right time to catch the sun beaming through the narrow opening to the larger cavern further in. I couldn't find mention of a name or the existence of this cave online, so called it the Cave of Colours, titled for the magical ability of the cave to glow brightly with the reflections off the clothes of whomever stood illuminated by the thin beam of sun. When one member of a rope team falls on a glacier or into a crevasse, it is up to the rest of the rope team to self arrest with their ice axes and hold the fallen member. For this exercise, the person leading the rope team would have to attempt a self arrest, while the other 2 members would run the other way down the glacier to simulate the forces of a crevasse fall.

Above: Probably the most spectacular sunrise I have ever witnessed. I woke up early, as I usually do for this very reason when on top of mountains, to see the sunrise. Katie and I were stunned to see that the clouds had become an ocean just several hundred metres below us. The peak we were camped on had become its own little island.
The sun had yet to rise, and we watched the dawn hues fade as the sun got closer to the horizon. As it appeared quietly over the mountains in the distance, rays of gold illuminated the tips of the clouds in their own ocean, like the crests of waves. The sun continued to spill golden light as it rose for the day, and the clouds got ever brighter as they swirled.
